Chapter.Content: 07 — The Rendering Equation and Path Probabilities
Reading map · Previous chapter · Next chapter

The rendering equation expresses outgoing radiance as an integral over incoming directions. Monte Carlo paths estimate that integral, so probability and estimator structure are part of the rendering model.
By the end: Interpret path contributions and their probability weights in a Monte Carlo renderer.
Recall question: Why must the probability density accompany a sampled light-transport path?
The rendering equation and light transport
Follow one path without losing its probability
Reconstruction checkpoint — isolate estimator invariants before tracing a scene

The path-transport chapter now has a small statistical witness independent of geometry. tools/labs/monte_carlo_transport_lab.cpp samples a cosine-weighted hemisphere and checks the analytic mean ; evaluates a Lambertian surface under a constant environment where cancels to the exact answer; runs a large deterministic Russian-roulette experiment and verifies survival compensation preserves expectation; and checks the balance-heuristic weight partition for two proposals.

This does not yet claim a complete path tracer, next-event estimator or participating-media renderer. It proves the sampling identities that a complete implementation depends on, so a later image disagreement can be separated into sampling math, scene intersection, BSDF evaluation, light PDFs and visibility. Use Multiple importance sampling, Russian roulette path termination and Sampling support and missing strata for the compact failure-oriented derivations.

A ray query answers where a line segment or half-line meets geometry. A renderer uses many such queries to evaluate light transport. At a diffuse panel hit, the camera path can sample another direction. At the lamp, it can collect emission. At glass, it must also know which two media meet at the boundary. Reflection, transmission and medium absorption are different terms in that transport calculation.

The sampling density must match the integration measure. If a lamp point is sampled uniformly over area , its area density is . Seen from a shading point at distance , that becomes directional density

If one of several lights is first chosen with probability , multiply by as well. For , , light cosine and , the final density is . A density greater than one is valid; it is probability per unit solid angle. Omitting the discrete selection probability makes the result depend incorrectly on the number of lights.

Multiple importance sampling, or MIS, combines estimates produced by different sampling techniques. For one light sample and one BSDF sample, power weights use their squared densities at the same possible contribution. BSDF means bidirectional scattering distribution function; unlike BRDF, the wider term also includes transmission. Both techniques must contribute their estimators. Multiplying the light estimate by a weight below one and omitting the BSDF counterpart generally loses expected energy. When a BSDF-sampled continuation reaches an emitter, the renderer must use the complementary weight when the light technique could also have generated that path. A delta event, such as ideal mirror reflection, uses a separate discrete-event treatment rather than an ordinary finite solid-angle density. PBRT’s complete path integrator
First-use completion — construct the two estimators and prove what MIS preserves
At this hit point the desired reflected direct-light integral is

Here is the incoming solid-angle direction, is incoming radiance in that direction, is the scattering function evaluated between the outgoing and incoming directions, is the surface normal, and is the visibility indicator (one if the sampled light path is unobstructed, zero otherwise). The absolute cosine is appropriate for a declared scattering domain that includes transmission; reflective-only code may instead use the positive hemisphere. Every probability density in the following formula is per unit solid angle at this same shading point. A light’s area density cannot be compared numerically to a BSDF’s directional density until the area-to-direction Jacobian has been applied.

Two algorithms can sample this integral. A light sampler chooses an emitter, a point on it, and the direction ; it must account for the discrete probability of selecting the emitter, area density on the chosen surface, and the change of measure from area to solid angle. A BSDF sampler chooses a direction based on the material’s scattering distribution, and then traces that direction to discover whether it reaches a light. Their directional probability densities are and . Neither technique needs to be uniformly good: light sampling helps with small visible emitters, while BSDF sampling helps with narrow glossy lobes.

The essential derivation is an expectation, not an appeal to intuition:

This cancellation assumes every nonzero contribution has support from at least one technique, densities are evaluated in a compatible measure, the chosen weights sum to one on supported paths, and the samples belong to the distributions claimed. A missing BSDF estimator breaks the second integral, so it is not enough to copy only the MIS weight into the light estimator. When the implementation uses one next-event-estimation sample and a BSDF-sampled continuation instead of explicitly drawing two samples in one function, the emitter-hit logic must still account for the complementary contribution at the correct path vertex.

The exponent 2 is a heuristic choice to suppress large weights from poorly matched samplers; it is not required by the unbiasedness proof. If the two techniques take and samples, the weights must account for their sample counts (for example by comparing and ), and each group is averaged with its corresponding sample count. The zero-density cases require an explicit policy: where but , assign all weight to B. Where both densities are zero and , neither estimator can represent the contribution and the sampling design is incomplete.

A light-technique observation at this point contributes ; a BSDF-technique observation there contributes . These are per-sample terms, not a demand that a single realization sum to one. Their expected values, integrated under their respective sampling densities, sum to the true . Chapter.Content: The pseudocode names the two probability contributions; it is not a drop-in path tracer. A real BSDF continuation carries throughput, medium state, visibility, path history, and an emission term that is already scaled consistently. For example, a perfectly specular delta event is a discrete probability mass and cannot be divided or compared as if it were an ordinary finite density over solid angle. A light directly visible from the camera, an environment emitter, and a path that reaches emission after several bounces need explicitly defined emission-handling branches to prevent both omission and double counting. Those implementation distinctions are required here, when MIS first affects the result, rather than being left as a promise of a future pass.

Scope of the retained path-loop examples. The supplied direct-light skeletons use max(dot(normal, wi), 0) and therefore implement reflective-hemisphere next-event estimation. A general BSDF with rough transmission can also contribute from the other hemisphere. It needs the appropriate absolute cosine, BSDF support, medium transition and visibility treatment. Keeping the reflective-only condition while advertising a complete transmissive estimator can omit light paths. The source code is retained for study, with this limitation made explicit.

Throughput stores the accumulated multiplicative transport weight along the camera path. At an ordinary sampled surface event it acquires . For Lambert reflection sampled with cosine density, this simplifies to reflectance . The cancellation is a useful implementation witness, not permission to omit densities for unrelated materials.

Russian roulette chooses whether to continue a path. With survival probability , multiply surviving throughput by . Its conditional expectation is unchanged because . Roulette changes variance and cost; a hard bounce cap still removes longer paths and generally introduces truncation bias. Refractive transport additionally needs a consistent index-of-refraction convention and medium state. A medium stack describes properly nested closed volumes; overlapping non-nested boundaries need a more explicit policy.
A missing region cannot be repaired by taking more samples there

Take the first five cells, in row-major order, of a jittered pixel grid. Four cells are never visited. Let the pixel integrand be , with rows counted upward from zero. The first three selected cells have expected , and the next two have expected . Equal averaging therefore gives

while the full pixel integral is . More repeated samples in those same cells converge to . The fix is a sampling design that covers the target domain with the appropriate weights, not simply more samples. This example corrects the supplied non-square-grid discussion.

The figure compares three distinct errors: interpolating the wrong projected quantity, averaging encoded light values, and omitting part of the sampling domain. Each panel uses the numerical witness derived above. The right panel numbers rows from bottom to top; another row orientation changes the biased value but does not restore full support.

For a reproducible renderer, associate random dimensions with pixel, sample and bounce identity rather than worker identity. Scheduling can then change without intentionally changing the sample set. Bitwise equality additionally requires a stable arithmetic and reduction order. A stochastic convergence plot should state its metric: ordinary finite-variance independent sampling gives mean-square error proportional to and root-mean-square error proportional to . A noisy reference, correlated samples or estimator bias can obscure those slopes.

The arrow from scattering back to the next interaction carries a ray, throughput, medium state and sampling history. Losing any of those can change the represented transport, even when every individual intersection test is correct.
